title: Striped garter triangle shawl
subtitle: A top-down triangle with two-colour horizontal garter stripes.
excerpt: A top-down triangular shawl in DK wool with horizontal two-colour garter stripes, worked flat from a garter-tab cast-on to a wingspan of 145 cm. Stripes alternate every 6 rows, so colour changes happen at the start of a right-side row and both yarns can be carried up the edge. About 200 g of each of two DK yarns.
sourceNotes: Horizontal stripe technique in a top-down triangle follows Zimmermann's top-down construction (Knitting Without Tears, 1971) with striping adapted from standard flat-knitting stripe practice. No single period source.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked.
knitting.finishedSizeText: Wingspan 145 cm. Centre-back depth 68 cm. Blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small strip of garter stitch worked on a few stitches, then rotated so live stitches can be picked up from all three edges, giving a neat triangular start at the centre back neck.

In flat-knit stripe work, the non-active yarn is left hanging at the edge rather than cut. After 6 or fewer rows the inactive colour is simply picked up at the start of its next stripe. Longer floats (more than 8 rows) should be caught at the edge every 4 rows to avoid loose loops at the side.

content.text: A top-down triangular shawl in two-colour DK wool, with horizontal garter stripes alternating every 6 rows. Knit flat from a three-stitch centre back to a wingspan of 145 cm.

The construction is the same top-down triangle as a plain garter shawl: four increases on every right-side row, knit every row. Colour changes happen every 6 rows at the start of a right-side row, so only one yarn is ever active at a time. Because the stripes are 6 rows apart, both yarns can be carried up the same edge without cutting. Budget about 200 g (440 m / 480 yards) of each colour in DK wool. The striped surface reads as horizontal bands across the blocked triangle and makes the best use of two complementary colours in a single skein each.
What you need

items.name: Colour A
items.qty: About 200 g (440 m / 480 yards) of DK-weight yarn

items.name: Colour B
items.qty: About 200 g (440 m / 480 yards) of DK-weight yarn, contrasting colour

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 80 cm or longer

content.text: Gauge

22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, blocked. Swatch in whichever colour you find tighter. Garter stripe tension tends to run more consistently than single-colour garter because alternate rows are worked with a different yarn and the tension averages out. If your blocked swatch reads 24 stitches per 10 cm, the finished wingspan will be about 133 cm at the same row count. Move to 4.5 mm needles if your gauge is tight.
Stitches used

items.name: yo
items.qty: yarn over: bring yarn forward and over needle. Adds one stitch.

content.text: Pattern
Garter tab cast-on
Work the
garter tab

in colour A. Cast on 3 stitches with waste yarn, knit 6 rows, switch to colour A, then pick up 9 stitches total as described in the plain garter triangle pattern. Knit 1 WS row with colour A and place 3 markers.
Stripe sequence and increase section
Work in 6-row stripes, alternating CA and CB. Both colours can be
carried up the edge
at the left selvedge, catching the unused yarn loosely every second row.
RS (increase row): k1, yo, SM, k to 1 st before spine marker, yo, k1, SM, k1, yo, SM, k to last st, yo, k1. (4 sts increased)
WS: k all sts.
Within each 6-row stripe: 3 RS increase rows and 3 WS plain knit rows. Colour changes happen at the start of every 7th row (the first RS of the new stripe). Continue until wingspan reaches 145 cm.
Stitch count check-ins
After 10 complete 6-row stripes (60 rows, 30 RS increase rows): 9 + 120 = 129 stitches. The wingspan is about 45 cm and the work sits clearly triangular.
After 25 complete stripes (150 rows, 75 RS increase rows): 9 + 300 = 309 stitches. Wingspan about 113 cm. Final target is approximately 170 RS increase rows at gauge.
Bind off
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off in whichever colour finishes the last stripe. A standard bind-off here fights the blocked wingspan and leaves the edge 10 to 15 cm shorter than pinned.
Common faults
Colour floats loose at the edge: the inactive colour was carried up without being caught. Catch it every 4 rows on the wrong side at the left selvedge to keep the edge tidy.
Stripe width uneven: the yarn was switched mid-row rather than at the start of a RS row. Always change colour at the start of a new right-side row so the stripe edge runs clean across the full width.

Jog at the colour change visible on the right side: garter stripes don't jog the way stocking stitch stripes do, because the first WS row of a new stripe knits back over the colour-change edge and buries it. If a jog is visible, the colour was changed on a WS row rather than an RS row.
Blocking

Soak in cool water, press out in towels, pin to wingspan 145 cm and depth 68 cm on a blocking mat. Stripe colours sometimes bleed slightly when first wet-blocked. Soak with colours face down on a white towel to check for bleeding before blocking on the mat.
Care
Hand wash in cool water with a wool-safe detergent. Lay flat to dry. If the two colours have not been pre-washed together, wash separately the first time to check for dye bleed.
What to try next

Three colours in the same stripe sequence gives a fade or a gradient effect when the colours are graded from light to dark. Working one colour for the first third of the shawl, introducing a second, then transitioning to a third across the remaining two thirds produces a smooth gradient without needing a hand-dyed skein.
